Susan Sontag wrote something in her book, On Photography. 

“The individual who seeks to record cannot intervene, and that the person who intervenes cannot then faithfully record, for the two aims contradict each other.” 

Although she was writing about the act of photographically documenting events and the importance of remaining uninvolved while doing so, I find this quote to be incredibly applicable to me and my circumstances. 

In the history of #MeToo, I am the one who intervened. 

I’m not a victim of sexual predation, I’m not a perpetrator, and I’m not one of the investigative reporters who broke the story of Harvey Weinstein’s decades of sexual misconduct in the entertainment industry. 

Like a person who has had a life event or a unique condition that takes over or comes to characterize their life in ways that others are unable to fully comprehend, what happened as a result of my #MeToo comment has imprinted itself upon me with an unmistakable self awareness that I am most certainly a person who intervened in the ongoing public drama of Harvey Weinstein and his many victims.

I’m equally repelled by the thought that I have to continue my to hear my own voice telling this story as I do this work.

I have very mixed feelings (and suspicions) about a LAW (!) regarding sexual misconduct that exists for one year only. But if there’s anyone that #MeToo was intended to help rescue from the career situations obliquely described by the young people in this video, it is models and actresses just like them. 

Neither laws nor powerful justice movements should be deployed as weapons to target anyone’s enemies, political or otherwise. Due process and fairness are essential because there are those among us who will abuse anything that can be abused and a system that is abused creates its own victims. The backlash against #MeToo is the result of such abuses. 

But it is undoubtedly true that the general public does not really understand what goes on and is tolerated as routine behaviors inside the media and entertainment empires that are responsible for everything they see on movie screens, on television, or in fashion magazines, etc. 

Look at these beautiful kids in this video. They are all someone’s daughters and sons. If you don’t think they would be targets of sexual predators in their work environments or that they are uniquely vulnerable to workplace harassment and abuses while trying to succeed in the industry they’re so perfectly suited for then you should open your mind and consider the realities of these media and entertainment industries which you have been hearing about since #MeToo in 2017 and even long before. 

When one of these models says in the video that the truth is they’ve all experienced the misconduct they are speaking out against, you should do some rough math in your head. All means everyone and I certainly don’t doubt her. 

I don’t know about the Adult Survivors Act in terms of it always (in the one short year that it will be in effect) being used appropriately. I would love to see some numbers on how many cases have been filed in comparison to the avalanche that was predicted. There has been one very famous case but I doubt there has been an avalanche. But no law passed to provide legal redress and, it should be hoped, legal protections, to victims of sexual crimes should exist for only one year. How is everyone then protected under the law and how under such a short rush of legally unique circumstances can you possibly ensure fairness and due process to both victims and accused? 

But I must confess, I would love to see a body of cases brought by models and actresses who have the solid evidence required to secure justice against the powerful predators in their respective industries. As I have said many times before, I had hoped that #MeToo would bring about changes in the laws surrounding workplace sexual misconduct that were specifically tailored to the unique circumstances of the entertainment and media industries. The Adult Survivors Act doesn’t remotely address what I had in mind and that shouldn’t be a surprise to anyone. 

The idea behind #MeToo was that a public response from women who had been victimized by sexual misconduct in pursuit of their careers in Hollywood would be so large and the shared stories so awful that there would be public outrage so powerful that it resulted in laws being enacted specifically designed to protect those who work in these powerful industries. 

None of that has happened and now I fully and painfully realize what a silly naive dreamer of a man I was one October morning in 2017. 

If you’ve got a solid case, file it. But remember, every bad case hurts #MeToo and this law wouldn’t even have come into existence without #MeToo and you wouldn’t be speaking out right now if #MeToo hadn’t happened. 

Sorry if that’s not the super supportive pat on the head you’ve probably come to expect from those on your side. I’m on the side of anyone who has been victimized sexually anywhere. But hard conversations have to be had.
